prompt:
A densely annotated editorial infographic plate, drawn by hand in confident ink
line with light watercolour and gouache wash on bright warm-white paper.
Contour line varies in weight and is charcoal near-black. Dimensional but not
photographic: restrained hatching, subtle texture, believable volume, selective
shadow, clean uncluttered background. Every material reads as itself — dull grey
lead, unglazed earthenware, weathered timber, damp fibrous bark — and materials
that differ in the explanation look visibly different. Quiet palette of stone,
clay, wood, and metal tones over the warm-white ground, with one or two
desaturated accents that each keep a single meaning throughout the plate.
Contemporary editorial typography: one calm display face for the title, one
highly legible face for the many small labels, sentence case, crisply printed
and correctly spelled. Annotation is dense and disciplined — leader lines,
brackets, dimension marks, magnified inset circles, small side studies — laid
out so no two leaders cross. Asymmetric composition with about a quarter of the
page left quiet. Modern printing on clean stock: fresh, crisp, and unaged. The
only lettering anywhere on the plate is the title, the deck, the labels, and the
short notes. The words hero, drawing, figure, plate, inset, zone, band, strip,
trio, column, and cutaway describe the construction of the page and are never
lettered onto it, alone or in a phrase: no headings that name parts of the
layout, no percentages or
proportions of the page, no tags in brackets after a label or note, no sentence
describing the drawing or explaining what the reader is meant to see, no
signature, monogram, date, watermark, or credit line.

Title, set largest at the top left of the page: planbook
Deck beneath it: A drawer of loose notes goes in; one book plan in the house shape comes out — thesis, storyline, and a chapter table the mill can read.

Hero: a foundry scene for paper. On the left, an open drawer overflows with unlike scraps — a torn notebook page, an index card, a folded letter, a small list — drifting up and into the mouth of a casting funnel drawn as a generous copper hopper. A note at the drawer: everything in the origins folder is read — notes, sketches, fragments, research. Beside the hopper a small leather-bound reference stands open on a stand, labeled an example plan, with a note: an earlier plan may stand by as the shape to match.

The hopper feeds a single elegant casting frame at the centre — a rectangular mould whose interior is divided like a printer's chase into the fixed shape of the house plan: a wide top bar for the title, a paragraph block labeled thesis, a slim slot labeled the storyline in one sentence, then a long ruled grid of many identical rows, and a small closing block labeled summary. The molten material filling the mould is drawn as flowing warm-toned script settling into the compartments. A note at the mould: the shape never varies; only the book changes.

At the right, the finished cast plan stands cooling on a rack — a crisp document titled Plan for the Quaker Detective, its chapter table visible as tidy rows. A slender arrow leads from it off the right edge toward a small scaffold frame on the horizon, captioned: the scaffold reads these rows next; each row becomes an essay's stub.

Two quiet details along the bottom:
- lower left: a small side spout on the hopper diverting into a shallow tray where the unmelted prompt lies as plain readable sheets, captioned — a dry run pours nothing: it shows the exact prompt and spends not a penny;
- lower right: a modest open ledger with one fresh entry, captioned — the one casting is paid for and entered in the shared ledger.

One warm accent colour follows the flowing material from drawer to mould to finished plan; the foundry ironwork and the reference book stay in ink.
